planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in early summer, or set out container-grown plants in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun to light shade in spring or fall; choose a sheltered site away from cold winter sun and wind, since the flower buds set the prior summer are sensitive to late freezes and bud injury.

directions: This Korean monotypic shrub in the olive family is grown for its almond-scented, star-shaped white flowers that open along the bare stems in very early spring, often weeks ahead of true forsythia and before the small, rounded leaves emerge. The four-petaled blossoms are borne in short axillary racemes along the previous year's wood and sometimes carry a faint pink or lilac flush, especially as they age. Growth habit is low and rangy, with arching, sprawling branches that benefit from occasional thinning right after bloom to maintain a tidier shape, since flower buds form on new growth produced that same season. Plant it where the early flowers can be appreciated up close, such as near a walkway or against a dark backdrop, and protect it from the harshest winter exposure to reduce bud loss in cold climates.

planting.note: Propagate by semi-hardwood cuttings in summer and plant container-grown stock in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade in spring or fall, siting it out of harsh winter wind and direct winter sun to protect the early flower buds.

directions: This selection of the Korean white forsythia replaces the species' typical white petals with a soft, consistent pink-to-rose coloring on the same small, four-petaled, almond-scented flowers that cover the bare arching branches in late winter to early spring. Because it blooms reliably true pink rather than the occasional faint blush seen on seedling-grown straight species plants, it is the form most often sought out for a distinct color note at the start of the flowering season. Habit, bloom timing, and culture otherwise mirror the species, with the shrub forming a low, loosely arching mound that benefits from light renewal pruning immediately after flowering to encourage the next year's bud-bearing shoots.
